nodes.content: Develop an image segmentation model that distinguishes genuine boundary ambiguity from unfamiliar anatomy under acquisition-domain shift.
requirements: Achieve unfamiliar-anatomy detection AUROC ≥0.85 on held-out acquisition domains.
Achieve boundary-uncertainty Spearman correlation ≥0.6 with inter-annotator disagreement while matching a supervised baseline’s Dice.

nodes.content: Train a Dice-regularized multi-annotator segmenter with style-invariant anatomy prototypes, scoring boundary disagreement separately from prototype-distance novelty.
Can style-invariant prototypes distinguish unfamiliar anatomy from familiar structures altered by held-out scanner contrast?
Style-invariant prototypes achieve unfamiliar-anatomy AUROC ≥0.85 on held-out scanners, with familiar-anatomy FPR ≤10% at 80% sensitivity.
Evaluate prototype-distance novelty on leave-one-scanner-out brain MRI with resection cavities; report AUROC and familiar-anatomy FPR at 80% sensitivity.
Leave-one-scanner-out brain MRI yielded cavity-detection AUROC 0.88 and familiar-anatomy FPR 8% at 80% sensitivity.
Retain prototype-distance novelty scoring for held-out scanners; cavity AUROC 0.88 and familiar-anatomy FPR 8% meet detection criteria.
Retaining prototype novelty scoring, calibrate boundary uncertainty against annotator disagreement on held-out scanners; compare Spearman correlation and Dice with U-Net.
Fit isotonic boundary-uncertainty calibration on multi-annotator brain MRI, then compare held-out-scanner disagreement Spearman and Dice against supervised U-Net.
BrainMRI-Cal v1 packages prototype novelty scoring, isotonic boundary calibration, and held-out-scanner Spearman and Dice comparisons against U-Net.
Using BrainMRI-Cal v1, audit held-out-scanner uncertainty–disagreement Spearman and U-Net-relative Dice, stratified by distance from resection cavities.
Held-out-scanner boundary-disagreement Spearman was 0.65 overall and 0.62 near cavities; Dice matched U-Net at 0.87.
On paired cross-scanner MRI, familiar-tissue prototype distances change <15%, while cavity distances remain ≥2× matched-tissue distances.
On paired same-patient cross-scanner MRIs, measure familiar-tissue prototype-distance shifts and cavity-to-matched-tissue distance ratios.
Paired cross-scanner MRIs showed 24% median familiar-tissue distance shifts, exceeding 15%, despite cavity-to-tissue distance ratios of 2.3×.
Can scanner-conditioned prototype alignment reduce familiar-tissue distance shifts below 15% without lowering cavity-detection AUROC below 0.85?
Fit scanner-conditioned prototype alignment using unlabeled normal-tissue MRIs, then measure paired-scanner distance shifts and held-out cavity AUROC.
Scanner-conditioned alignment reduced median familiar-tissue distance shifts from 24% to 11%; held-out cavity-detection AUROC was 0.86.
Train a dual-head segmenter combining annotator-distribution boundary entropy with scanner-style-normalized normalizing-flow novelty scores.
Train the dual-head flow model on multi-annotator brain MRI; compare held-out-scanner cavity AUROC, boundary-disagreement Spearman, and Dice against BrainMRI-Cal v1.
Use the alignment validated by e4 to train the dual-head flow model and measure held-out-scanner cavity AUROC.
FlowSeg v1 checkpoint contains the trained dual-head segmenter, scanner-conditioned alignment, and held-out-scanner cavity-AUROC evaluation scripts.
Can FlowSeg v1 exceed aligned-prototype cavity AUROC 0.86 while retaining boundary-disagreement Spearman ≥0.6 and Dice ≥0.87?
FlowSeg v1 achieves held-out-scanner cavity AUROC ≥0.89, boundary-disagreement Spearman ≥0.60, and Dice ≥0.87.
Evaluate FlowSeg v1 on held-out-scanner MRI, measuring cavity AUROC, boundary-disagreement Spearman, and Dice against aligned prototypes and U-Net.
Held-out-scanner FlowSeg v1 achieved cavity AUROC 0.90 and Dice 0.87, but boundary-disagreement Spearman reached only 0.53.
Freeze FlowSeg’s encoder and nonboundary heads; ranking-loss fine-tuning raises boundary Spearman ≥0.60, preserving cavity AUROC ≥0.89 and Dice ≥0.87.
Freeze FlowSeg’s encoder and nonboundary heads; fine-tune the boundary head with disagreement-ranking loss, then measure Spearman, cavity AUROC, and Dice.
Ranking-loss fine-tuning raised held-out-scanner boundary Spearman from 0.53 to 0.63; cavity AUROC remained 0.90 and Dice 0.87.
Compare ranking-tuned FlowSeg against BrainMRI-Cal v1 on identical held-out scanners, measuring cavity AUROC, boundary-disagreement Spearman, Dice, and uncertainty cross-talk.
On identical held-out scanners, cavity-core boundary-ambiguity false positives were 31% for BrainMRI-Cal versus 8% for FlowSeg, with Dice 0.87.
Choose FlowSeg over BrainMRI-Cal: Spearman 0.63 versus 0.65 and Dice 0.87, but cavity-core ambiguity false positives fall 31%→8%.
Train a scanner-counterfactual diffusion segmenter that estimates boundary ambiguity from annotator variance and anatomical novelty from style-invariant reconstruction residuals.
Can scanner-counterfactual diffusion reduce familiar-tissue novelty false positives on unseen scanners without missing small resection cavities?
Using scanner alignment validated by e4, train counterfactual diffusion; compare unseen-scanner familiar-tissue false positives and sub-10-mm cavity sensitivity against FlowSeg.
On unseen scanners, diffusion cut familiar-tissue FPR from FlowSeg’s 9% to 5%; sub-10-mm cavity sensitivity rose from 78% to 81%.
Does diffusion-derived boundary uncertainty achieve disagreement Spearman ≥0.60 while maintaining Dice ≥0.87 on held-out scanners?
Counterfactual diffusion achieves held-out-scanner boundary-disagreement Spearman ≥0.60 and Dice ≥0.87, matching ranking-tuned FlowSeg.
Using aligned diffusion from e8, evaluate annotator-variance boundary maps against disagreement and Dice on held-out scanners, alongside ranking-tuned FlowSeg.
Held-out-scanner diffusion achieved boundary-disagreement Spearman 0.49 and Dice 0.85, below FlowSeg’s 0.63 and 0.87 despite improved novelty FPR.
Retain FlowSeg; defer diffusion despite 5% familiar-tissue FPR because boundary Spearman 0.49 and Dice 0.85 miss targets.
Gate FlowSeg novelty alerts with scanner-counterfactual diffusion residuals, freezing its segmentation and calibrated boundary heads.
Calibrate diffusion-residual gating on validation scanners, then compare held-out cavity AUROC, familiar-tissue FPR, boundary Spearman, and Dice against FlowSeg.
Fit diffusion-residual gates on validation scanners with frozen FlowSeg heads; evaluate held-out cavity AUROC, familiar-tissue FPR, boundary Spearman, and Dice.
GatedFlowSeg v1 packages frozen FlowSeg heads, scanner-counterfactual novelty gates, and held-out-scanner cavity AUROC, FPR, Spearman, and Dice reports.
Audit GatedFlowSeg v1 against ranking-tuned FlowSeg on held-out scanners, including cavity AUROC, familiar-tissue FPR, boundary Spearman, and Dice.
Held-out-scanner GatedFlowSeg achieved cavity AUROC 0.89, familiar-tissue FPR 6% versus FlowSeg’s 9%, boundary Spearman 0.63, and Dice 0.87.
Compare GatedFlowSeg against retained FlowSeg by scanner and cavity size; audit novelty FPR, cavity-core cross-talk, AUROC, Spearman, and Dice.
Across scanners, GatedFlowSeg reduced familiar-tissue FPR from 8–11% to 5–7%; sub-10-mm cavity sensitivity remained 78%.
Adopt GatedFlowSeg: FPR falls 9%→6%, AUROC reaches 0.89, Spearman 0.63, and Dice 0.87; diffusion’s lower FPR sacrifices segmentation.
After adopting GatedFlowSeg, test independent vendor-scanner cohorts with multiple annotations; report cavity AUROC, boundary Spearman, and Dice versus U-Net.
Using GatedFlowSeg v1, evaluate independent vendor-scanner cohorts with multiple annotations; measure cavity AUROC, boundary Spearman, and U-Net-relative Dice.
VendorShift audit v1 contains independent-cohort cavity AUROC, annotation-disagreement Spearman, and U-Net-relative Dice tables by scanner vendor.
